items.title: Next.js: Information disclosure across root params when a 'use cache' function is called through unstable_cache()
items.text: Next.js applications with `'use cache'` can disclose cached data across root params when the same `'use cache'` function is called both directly during rendering and through `unstable_cache()`, and that function reads a root param. Root params are route parameters of the root layout, and applications commonly use them to scope data, for example per locale. During a cold process start, a cross-request deduplication race allowed an `unstable_cache()` call to join the in-flight fill of a concurrent direct call and receive its result, bypassing the root param check that would normally reject it. `unstable_cache()` then stored that result under a cache key without root params, so subsequent requests for other root param values received the same entry until it is revalidated or evicted. Cached data produced for one root param value is returned to requests for other values. Exploitation requires the `unstable_cache()` request to arrive while the function's first fill after a process start is still in flight. Outside this race, the nesting already throws an error: `'use cache' inside unstable_cache() is unsupported`, and avoiding it is a complete workaround.

items.title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
items.text: Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done. Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: , , , and .DiscoverySelectionAccessSuccess You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, : whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly.Success That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change. That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one. items.title: pnpm Introduces New Lockfile Format to Reduce Git Merge Conflicts
items.text: pnpm has introduced an experimental lockfile format designed to reduce Git merge conflicts by changing how dependency relationships are recorded. The new format, available starting with pnpm 12.19.0, previews changes planned for pnpm 13 and is available as an opt-in setting. The change addresses a common frustration in JavaScript development, particularly in projects with multiple contributors or large dependency trees. Updates to dependencies can produce substantial changes in pnpm-lock.yaml, creating merge conflicts when developers work on separate branches. The new format aims to reduce those conflicts by keeping related dependency information together and limiting the number of lines affected when peer dependencies change. # The existing v9 lockfile format uses separate packages and snapshots sections to store package metadata and resolved dependency relationships. The experimental v13 format consolidates that information into a single packages section. The top-level importers section is also renamed to projects.
